parts: A transition is a process — a period of change from one situation to another. The home-to-school transition is the move from home to preschool (usually around age three) or from preschool to primary school. It can be critical: poor transitions are linked to less successful outcomes, poor attendance and disengagement. Children from deprived backgrounds, with special needs, with poor socio-emotional skills or low self-esteem, and those who never attended an anganwadi, balwadi or preschool find it harder. Parents also find transitions stressful; school support and advance information reduce their stress. Gradual change and familiarisation help; a sudden switch to formal teaching, less play and fewer child-initiated activities makes it harder. Trusting relationships with familiar adults give children security to explore new places.

Success depends on the child's own characteristics (temperament, personality), the parents' characteristics (awareness, education, attitude to school) and the community's (access to and quality of local services). Transition is harder for financially disadvantaged, indigenous, culturally and linguistically diverse families and families of children with a disability. Important for success: building on children's prior practices, giving children an active role with their families, helping them understand the routines of the new setting, helping them handle changes in status and identity, and working collaboratively; a partnership between parents and educators helps parents manage the change. Smooth transition depends on family-school, child-school, peer and community connections.

Ideas: children visit the centre and meet their future teacher; visit the school for special events; parents practise school-type activities (walking in a line, kindergarten songs and games) and make scrapbooks with photos of the teacher and building. An ideal support system has supportive communities, strong families (the child's first teacher), quality early care and education, prepared schools and ready children. Parents can visit the centre, show where the washrooms are, find out about lunch, read books about kindergarten and answer questions simply. Schools can offer orientation — meeting teachers and staff, visiting classrooms and the playground — and children can practise skills such as packing a bag, toileting, fastening clothes, washing hands and opening lunch boxes; stories with photos also help.

Signs of a successful transition: children like school and look forward to it, show steady academic growth; parents are actively involved; classrooms create positive feelings; teachers, staff and families value one another; cultural diversity is celebrated; developmentally appropriate practice is visible.

School readiness is many-sided — physical health, social and emotional development, language, literacy and cognition — and schools too must be ready for children and families. Earlier it was judged only by age or by measured skills; now all aspects of development are considered. Readiness is the academic knowledge, independence, communication and social skills a child needs to do well in school. Levels: demonstrating, approaching and emerging readiness (the last two need instructional support). Dimensions: approaches to learning, cognition and general knowledge, language, physical well-being, social and emotional development. A school-ready child is independent in toileting, can dress, understands expected behaviour, is confident, takes turns and shares, sits still for a short time and can separate from parents.

Components of readiness for preschool: academic readiness (basic knowledge of self, family and world — reading daily, library visits, rhymes, name in print, colours, puzzles, outings); social readiness (getting along, following directions, taking turns, saying goodbye to parents — rules, routines, play with others); independence (self-help tasks like zipping and buttoning, simple chores, toileting); communication skills (conversation, listening, new words, songs); health and physical well-being (balanced diet, rest, medical and dental care, immunisation, large- and small-muscle activities).

Readiness for school (more formal than preschool): emotional and social preparation (following rules and routines, expressing needs, curiosity, working alone, being away from parents without upset, focusing and listening) and language, maths and general knowledge (five-to-six-word sentences, rhymes, writing name and address, counting, shapes and colours, print versus pictures, concepts of time, sorting and classifying). Key indicators: readiness to accept responsibility and independence, enthusiasm for learning, and ability to make friends and respect others.
Roles of parents, schools and teachers

Ready children: the teacher observes whether each child demonstrates, approaches or shows emerging readiness and plans activities accordingly — a continuous process. Ready parents, families and communities: mothers and family are the first teachers; they give steady, supportive relationships, age-appropriate toys and a loving home, make sure children are toilet-trained and can express their needs; communities open quality day-care centres and support anganwadi workers. Ready schools: involve parents and crèche workers, share preschool portfolios with the grade one teacher, respect individual differences, provide child-friendly toilets, accessible shelves, a print-rich classroom with displays at children's eye level and enough materials; the ECCE centre is best located near the primary school. Ready teachers: understand development, observe well, give emotional security, keep a flexible, play-based programme, interact with primary teachers and keep upgrading their skills.

Language and cognition: free and guided conversation, stories and rhymes, structured and free play, riddles, role play, excursions. Reading readiness: visual and sound discrimination, observation and memory, classification, sequential thinking, vocabulary. Writing readiness: clay modelling, colouring within a space, drawing on a slate or floor, tracing, copying forms, joining dots, zig-zag and straight lines. Number readiness: classification, sequencing, problem solving and pre-number concepts. Physical-motor: games for health and social habits. Creative: colouring, drawing, crafts, tearing and pasting for muscle control. Skills should be introduced only when children are ready; pushing them early creates aversion and dropout.
